title: Thermal Expansion of Solids
short_intro: Thermal expansion of solids is the tendency of solid matter to change in volume, area, and length in response to a change in temperature. This phenomenon arises due to the asymmetry of the interatomic potential energy well and the increased anharmonicity of atomic vibrations at elevated temperatures.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Linear, superficial, and cubical expansion coefficients (alpha, beta, gamma), their interrelations, determination of expansion effects in simple structures, and pendulum clock time-loss problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Temperature dependence of expansion coefficients, anisotropic expansion in non-cubic crystals, stress and strain generated by thermal constraints, and thermal bending of bimetallic strips.

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Origin of Thermal Expansion
bullets: Solids consist of atoms vibrating about their equilibrium positions inside an asymmetric potential well.
As temperature rises, the total vibrational energy increases, raising the average interatomic distance due to the steeper repulsive wall compared to the attractive wall.
Harmonic approximation yields zero thermal expansion; anharmonicity of lattice vibrations is strictly required for thermal expansion.

concept_notes.heading: Types of Thermal Expansion
bullets: Linear expansion refers to the fractional change in length per unit change in temperature, quantified by the coefficient of linear expansion (α).
Superficial (area) expansion refers to the fractional change in surface area per unit change in temperature, quantified by β.
Cubical (volume) expansion refers to the fractional change in volume per unit change in temperature, quantified by γ.

concept_notes.heading: Interrelation Between Expansion Coefficients
bullets: For isotropic solids, the coefficients are related by the standard geometric ratios: β = 2α and γ = 3α.
These relations are derived by neglecting higher-order terms of the expansion coefficient multiplied by the temperature change (ΔT).
For anisotropic crystals, expansion coefficients vary with crystallographic axes, leading to tensor representations of thermal expansion.

concept_notes.heading: Thermal Stress and Bimetallic Strips
bullets: If a solid is rigidly clamped and prevented from expanding or contracting, thermal stress develops inside the material, proportional to Young's modulus and the temperature change.
A bimetallic strip consists of two metals with different expansion coefficients riveted together, causing the strip to bend toward the metal with the lower coefficient upon heating.

derivations.title: Relation between Superficial and Linear Expansion Coefficients
derivations.conditions: Isotropic solid sheet undergoing a small uniform temperature change ΔT
steps: Consider a rectangular sheet of initial dimensions L<sub>0</sub> and breadth B<sub>0</sub> at temperature T<sub>0</sub>.
Upon heating by ΔT, the new dimensions become L = L<sub>0</sub>(1 + αΔT) and B = B<sub>0</sub>(1 + αΔT).
The new area A = L × B = L<sub>0</sub>B<sub>0</sub>(1 + αΔT)<sup>2</sup> = A<sub>0</sub>(1 + 2αΔT + α<sup>2</sup>(ΔT)<sup>2</sup>).
Neglecting the small second-order term α<sup>2</sup>(ΔT)<sup>2</sup>, we get A = A<sub>0</sub>(1 + 2αΔT).
By definition of superficial expansion, A = A<sub>0</sub>(1 + βΔT), therefore equating the coefficients gives β = 2α.

derivations.title: Thermal Stress in a Constrained Rod
derivations.conditions: A uniform metallic rod of length L, cross-sectional area A, and Young's modulus Y fixed rigidly between two immovable walls
steps: Let the temperature of the rod be increased by ΔT. If free, the expansion would be ΔL<sub>free</sub> = L α ΔT.
Since the walls prevent this expansion, a compressive strain is induced in the rod given by Strain = ΔL / L = α ΔT.
Using Hooke's law, Stress = Y × Strain = Y α ΔT.
The total compressive force (F) exerted by the rod on the walls is given by F = Stress × A = Y A α ΔT.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Interatomic Potential Energy vs Interatomic Distance
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An asymmetric potential well curve U(r) versus interatomic separation r, showing horizontal energy levels representing vibrational states.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The asymmetry of the well causes the mean separation (average of turning points) to shift to larger values as vibrational energy increases with temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical explanation of why solids expand when heated.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Length vs Temperature Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of length L versus temperature T with a positive slope equal to L<sub>0</sub>α.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the curve represents the absolute linear expansion rate for a given initial length.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Determining the coefficient of linear expansion from experimental data points.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searches' Apparatus / Pullinger's Apparatus
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of a metallic rod enclosed in a steam jacket with a micrometer screw gauge measuring linear expansion.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct measurement of expansion ΔL corresponding to steam temperature change enables precise evaluation of α.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Experimental determination and viva-voce questions on laboratory measurement of expansion coefficients.

solved_numericals.question: A metal rod of length 2 m at 20 °C is heated to 100 °C. If the coefficient of linear expansion of the metal is 1.2 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>, calculate the final length of the rod.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L<sub>0</sub> = 2 m, T<sub>1</sub> = 20 °C, T<sub>2</sub> = 100 °C, α = 1.2 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Calculate temperature change: ΔT = T<sub>2</sub> - T<sub>1</sub> = 100 - 20 = 80 °C (or K).
Apply linear expansion formula: L = L<sub>0</sub>(1 + αΔT).

solved_numericals.question: A brass rod of cross-sectional area 4 cm<sup>2</sup> is clamped firmly at both ends so that it cannot expand. If the temperature is raised by 50 °C, calculate the thermal force developed in the rod. (Given for brass: Y = 1.0 x 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>, α = 2.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: A = 4 cm<sup>2</sup> = 4 x 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, ΔT = 50 K, Y = 1.0 x 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>, α = 2.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Recall thermal force formula: F = Y A α ΔT.
Substitute the numerical values: F = (1.0 x 10<sup>11</sup>) x (4 x 10<sup>-4</sup>) x (2.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup>) x 50.
Calculate final force: F = 400 x 100 = 40,000 N = 4 x 10<sup>4</sup> N.

solved_numericals.question: A pendulum clock keeps correct time at 20 °C. The pendulum consists of a brass rod of linear expansion coefficient α = 1.9 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>. How much time will the clock lose or gain in one day if the room temperature rises to 40 °C?
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: α = 1.9 x 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>, ΔT = 40 - 20 = 20 K, Time in one day (t) = 24 x 3600 s.
Use fractional time loss relation: Δt / t = (1/2) α ΔT.
Substitute values: Δt = (1/2) x (1.9 x 10<sup>-5</sup>) x 20 x (86400).
Calculate intermediate product: (1/2) x 20 = 10; Δt = 1.9 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x 10 x 86400 = 1.9 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 86400.

assumptions_and_limitations: The coefficients of expansion (α, β, γ) are assumed to be constant over the moderate temperature range considered, whereas in reality, they depend slightly on temperature.
Higher-order terms in temperature change (such as α<sup>2</sup>(ΔT)<sup>2</sup>) are neglected under the assumption of small temperature variations (ΔT << 1 / α).
Isotropy is assumed for simple geometric relations between linear, superficial, and cubical expansion; anisotropic crystals require tensorial treatment.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A cavity or hole inside a solid object contracts when the solid object is heated.
common_misconceptions.correct: The hole expands in the exact same proportion as the surrounding solid material.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal expansion applies uniformly to all dimensions of the body, meaning empty space within the body expands as if it were filled with the solid.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Water exhibits regular thermal expansion behavior across all temperature ranges.
common_misconceptions.correct: Water exhibits anomalous expansion between 0 °C and 4 °C, contracting upon heating in this specific interval.
common_misconceptions.why: Due to hydrogen bonding and open cage-like molecular clustering, water has maximum density at 4 °C.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The coefficient of volume expansion is strictly three times the linear expansion coefficient for all materials.
common_misconceptions.correct: The relation γ = 3α holds strictly for isotropic solids; for anisotropic or single crystals, γ = α<sub>x</sub> + α<sub>y</sub> + α<sub>z</sub>.
common_misconceptions.why: Anisotropic media possess different expansion properties along orthogonal crystallographic axes.

quick_revision: The fundamental relations for isotropic solids are β = 2α and γ = 3α.
Thermal stress developed in a rigidly fixed rod is given by σ = YαΔT.
Density of a solid decreases with temperature according to ρ ≈ ρ<sub>0</sub>(1 - γΔT).
A pendulum clock runs slow (loses time) at higher temperatures because the pendulum rod expands, increasing its effective length and time period.
